# Draft:The Cultures Framework (a sustainability theory)

The Cultures Framework is an analytical framework used in sustainability studies to examine the relationship between culture and sustainability outcomes. It was developed by Janet Stephenson and collaborators, originally as the Energy Cultures Framework, and was first introduced in the academic literature in 2010. Early versions described energy behaviour through the interaction of cognitive norms, practices and material culture, while later versions reformulated the core elements as motivators, activities and materiality, and also incorporated agency, external influences and outcomes.
History
The framework emerged from interdisciplinary research on energy behaviour in New Zealand. In its initial formulation, the Energy Cultures Framework was intended to provide an integrating model for understanding energy behaviour and identifying possibilities for behaviour change. A 2015 article further elaborated the framework after several years of empirical use and conceptual development.
The framework was also extended beyond household energy use. In 2015, Stephenson, Debbie Hopkins and Adam Doering applied it to questions of transport transition.
In a 2018 article, Stephenson reframed the approach more explicitly as a contribution to cultural theory and sustainability research, referring to “sustainability cultures” rather than only “energy cultures”. In her 2023 book Culture and Sustainability, Stephenson presented the mature version as the more general Cultures Framework.
Overview
The framework treats culture as a dynamic ensemble rather than a static set of values. In its early form, it analysed the interaction of:
* cognitive norms
* energy practices
* material culture
In its later formulation, these became:
* motivators
* activities
* materiality
Later versions also emphasise:
* the agency of actors such as individuals, households, organisations, communities and governments
* external influences that may reinforce stability or enable change
* sustainability outcomes as the result of interactions within a cultural ensemble
Applications
The framework has been applied in studies of household energy use, transport, business energy efficiency, energy technologies and policy design.
Researchers outside Stephenson’s original team have also applied or adapted the framework in a range of settings, including industrial energy management, public perceptions of distributed energy storage in the United Kingdom, rural sustainability transitions in Transylvania, and household retrofit and sustainable energy policy analysis in Ireland.
Use and assessment
Independent scholars have described the framework as a useful heuristic for organising a wide range of social and material factors in energy research. It has also been characterised as a broad and integrative exploratory tool for interdisciplinary inquiry into energy transitions and sustainability outcomes. In a review of energy management research, Rotzek and colleagues argued that it provided a basis for further transdisciplinary collaboration and refinement in industrial contexts.
More broadly, reviews of culture and low-carbon transitions have situated energy-cultures research within a wider literature on cultural barriers to sustainability transitions.
